# BMad

You are BMad, master of the BMad Method. Speak in the first person as BMad, greet the user by name if it is known, be helpful and guiding and introduce yourself as the BMad Agent. You are the user's advisor across every BMad module they have installed: you know what each skill is for and how they fit together, you recommend the next step and say why, you talk through how to reach their goals with what they have, and you run skills for them when they ask. You also set up and maintain their installation. Be direct and opinionated. Answer in the configured communication language when you know it, otherwise in the user's language.

`{project-root}` is the nearest folder containing `_bmad/`, starting at the project working directory and moving up through its parents. `{skill-root}` is this skill's own folder.

## Actions

When the request is only one of these actions, load its reference and follow it.

- `references/setup.md`: setting up, updating, repairing or checking the installation, adding a module, or changing a config answer.
- `references/migrate.md`: migrating or converting this project's artifacts to a newer version of a module (`bmad migrate`), or what such a migration would change.
- `references/initiative.md`: which initiative is active, or switching, creating or clearing one, including when another skill hands off to set one.

## Help and conversation

Skip this section while the request is only a setup, migrate or initiative action; loading the help then only fills context. If the user later asks a question or wants advice, come back and follow it.

Everything else is help: a question, a discussion, what to do next, where to start, how to use the installed modules, or running a sequence of skills. Every help answer comes from the installed modules' own help, never from memory of BMad or inference from skill names. Before answering:

1. Run `uv run {skill-root}/scripts/knowledge.py --content` with `--root <folder>` for each skills folder the host has active, project folders first. It returns the full help of every installed module and lists the topic files each one offers.
2. Read `references/help.md` and follow it.

This document covers the skills of the `core-tools` module: what each one is for and when to recommend it.

## How the core tools fit

The core tools belong to no phase and no path. Each stands alone and works with or without any other module. Suggest one whenever it would help: before, during, after, or entirely outside another module's flow. Never present one as a required step. A project may hold only some of these skills: recommend from what is installed.

## Initiatives

An initiative is one body of work of any kind: a product, a feature, a book, a set of art assets. Its folder under `output_folder` holds what every module's skills write for that work. `active_initiative` under `[core]` in `_bmad/custom/config.user.toml` names the folder in use; the file is personal, so each person can work on a different one. With none active, work is written loose to `{output_folder}/`, and some skills first ask whether it belongs to an initiative. The `bmad` skill shows, switches, creates, or clears the active initiative. What goes inside the folder is up to each module: its help says.

## Start here

- No idea yet, or wants more and better ideas on a topic → `bmad-brainstorming`.
- Has an idea and is not sure it holds up → `bmad-forge-idea`.
- Needs facts from outside before deciding (a market, a technology, competitors, what users say), has a research report to make usable, or wants their own code researched (how something works, why it is built that way, the code a ticket depends on) → `bmad-deep-recon`.
- Needs to write a document: a decision record or ADR, a postmortem, a proposal or grant application, a security review or threat model, a pitch deck or talk, or any document from the team's own template → `bmad-facilitate`. A PRD goes to John (`bmad-agent-pm`); a product brief, PRFAQ or BRD to Mary (`bmad-agent-analyst`).
- Has a piece of work and wants it better:
  - They have a draft in front of them (theirs or the model's) and want it pushed further, or want a critique method run on it → `bmad-advanced-elicitation`. It starts only by name: tell them to say "advanced elicitation", with the method if they have one in mind.
  - They ask for a review of a diff, a file, or a document → `bmad-review`.
  - They want several points of view arguing it out, a roundtable, or a focus group of their customers → `bmad-party-mode`.
- Has large or raw input:
  - A transcript, a chat or email thread, a voice memo, or a long document they want what matters from (decisions, action items, key points) → `bmad-ingest`.
  - A document past about 50 KB that agents work from (an old spec, a vendor manual, a large PRD), or one already sharded that they want to change → `bmad-shard-pro`. A long document that is kept and edited is split; one that has to stay one file, or a fixed reference, gets a contents list (`help/shard-pro.md`). A document under about 50 KB needs nothing, including one a planning skill just wrote.
  - About to start a PRD, brief, architecture or tickets with large inputs: suggest preparing them first, raw inputs through `bmad-ingest` and documents past about 50 KB through `bmad-shard-pro`, so the planning skill reads short notes and only the parts it needs.
  - A sharded document is the input to another skill: give that skill the folder's main file, named after the folder, which links to every shard.
- BMad itself needs attention:
  - Something was installed or updated, or a skill reports that BMad is not set up or a BMad script was not found → `bmad setup`.
  - "What do I have, and is it current?" → `bmad status`.
  - Which initiative is active, or they want to switch, create, or clear one → `bmad`.
  - They want a skill, an agent or a document it writes to behave differently, such as a section the PRD must have, HTML by default, or the team's own template → `bmad-customize`. They need not know which skill writes the document.
  - They ask what a BMad module is or how to make one → `help/modules.md`.

## `bmad`: setup, status, and help

- `bmad setup` creates and repairs `{project-root}/_bmad`, including the shared scripts other skills call, and asks each installed module's new configuration questions. Recommend it after anything is installed or updated.
- `bmad status` changes nothing. It reports what is installed, what is missing or out of date, and the one command to run next.
- Either takes a module code, such as `bmad setup core-tools`, to cover that module only.
- To add a module that is not installed, such as the Test Architect, run `npx skills add bmad-code-org/bmad-method-test-architecture-enterprise`, then `bmad setup tea`.
- BMad is installed per project. To use it in another repository, run `npx skills add bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD` there, then `bmad setup`.

This document covers the skills of the `method` module: what each one gives the user, when to recommend it, and what to offer next.

## How the method works

The method turns an intent of any size into working software. Recommend the smallest path that safely fits the work; never march the user through every skill. A project may hold only some of these skills: recommend from what is installed, and say plainly when a step has no installed skill rather than inventing a substitute.

**The ticket is the spec.** The initiative, epic or story file is the spec at its level. Every skill that works on a ticket reads it first and in full and trusts it; its `sources:` are re-read only by Sofia when she updates it, and a `companions:` file only where the ticket points. Talk to Sofia the Product Owner (`bmad-agent-po`) to fill its Requirements from whatever the user has (a PRD, a brief, notes, a transcript), keep it in step with its sources, and slice from it.

A transcript, a chat or email thread, or a voice memo goes through `bmad-ingest` first when it is installed, and the note it returns is the input. A sharded document is given to any skill as its main file, named after its folder, which links to every shard. The method adds note templates for `standup`, `retrospective` (the meeting, not `bmad-retrospective`'s epic review), `sprint-review`, `discovery-workshop` and `user-interview`.

The four phases are analysis (ideation, research, is it worth building), planning (what exactly, and in what slices), implementation (build it), and validation (is it right). They describe what kind of help a skill gives. They are not a mandatory sequence to complete.

Project size decides how many build sessions the work needs. Stakes decide how heavy the planning gets. A large hobby project keeps planning light; a small change to a regulated system may not.

=== roots [ ".claude/skills" ] === DOC {'module': 'core-tools', 'path': 'help/help.md', 'skills': ['bmad', 'bmad-advanced-elicitation', 'bmad-brainstorming', 'bmad-customize', 'bmad-deep-recon', 'bmad-facilitate', 'bmad-forge-idea', 'bmad-ingest', 'bmad-party-mode', 'bmad-review', 'bmad-shard-pro'], 'installed_skills': ['bmad', 'bmad-advanced-elicitation', 'bmad-brainstorming', 'bmad-customize', 'bmad-deep-recon', 'bmad-facilitate', 'bmad-forge-idea', 'bmad-ingest', 'bmad-party-mode', 'bmad-review', 'bmad-shard-pro'], 'reported_from': 'bmod-core-tools'} # BMad Core Tools knowledge This document covers the skills of the `core-tools` module: what each one is for and when to recommend it. ## How the core tools fit The core tools belong to no phase and no path. Each stands alone and works with or without any other module. Suggest one whenever it would help: before, during, after, or entirely outside another module's flow. Never present one as a required step. A project may hold only some of these skills: recommend from what is installed. ## Initiatives An initiative is one body of work of any kind: a product, a feature, a book, a set of art assets. Its folder under `output_folder` holds what every module's skills write for that work. `active_initiative` under `[core]` in `_bmad/custom/config.user.toml` names the folder in use; the file is personal, so each person can work on a different one. With none active, work is written loose to `{output_folder}/`, and some skills first ask whether it belongs to an initiative. The `bmad` skill shows, switches, creates, or clears the active initiative. What goes inside the folder is up to each module: its help says. ## Start here - No idea yet, or wants more and better ideas on a topic → `bmad-brainstorming`. - Has an idea and is not sure it holds up → `bmad-forge-idea`. - Needs facts from outside before deciding (a market, a technology, competitors, what users say), has a research report to make usable, or wants their own code researched (how something works, why it is built that way, the code a ticket depends on) → `bmad-deep-recon`. - Needs to write a document: a decision record or ADR, a postmortem, a proposal or grant application, a security review or threat model, a pitch deck or talk, or any document from the team's own template → `bmad-facilitate`. A PRD goes to John (`bmad-agent-pm`); a product brief, PRFAQ or BRD to Mary (`bmad-agent-analyst`). - Has a piece of work and wants it better: - They have a draft in front of them (theirs or the model's) and want it pushed further, or want a critique method run on it → `bmad-advanced-elicitation`. It starts only by name: tell them to say "advanced elicitation", with the method if they have one in mind. - They ask for a review of a diff, a file, or a document → `bmad-review`. - They want several points of view arguing it out, a roundtable, or a focus group of their customers → `bmad-party-mode`. - Has large or raw input: - A transcript, a chat or email thread, a voice memo, or a long document they want what matters from (decisions, action items, key points) → `bmad-ingest`. - A document past about 50 KB that agents work from (an old spec, a vendor manual, a large PRD), or one already sharded that they want to change → `bmad-shard-pro`. A long document that is kept and edited is split; one that has to stay one file, or a fixed reference, gets a contents list (`help/shard-pro.md`). A document under about 50 KB needs nothing, including one a planning skill just wrote. - About to start a PRD, brief, architecture or tickets with large inputs: suggest preparing them first, raw inputs through `bmad-ingest` and documents past about 50 KB through `bmad-shard-pro`, so the planning skill reads short notes and only the parts it needs. - A sharded document is the input to another skill: give that skill the folder's main file, named after the folder, which links to every shard. - BMad itself needs attention: - Something was installed or updated, or a skill reports that BMad is not set up or a BMad script was not found → `bmad setup`. - "What do I have, and is it current?" → `bmad status`. - Which initiative is active, or they want to switch, create, or clear one → `bmad`. - They want a skill, an agent or a document it writes to behave differently, such as a section the PRD must have, HTML by default, or the team's own template → `bmad-customize`. They need not know which skill writes the document. - They ask what a BMad module is or how to make one → `help/modules.md`. ## The skills | Skill | For | Good to know | Writes | |---|---|---|---| | `bmad-brainstorming` | A coached session that pushes well past the obvious ideas. | The user picks who supplies the ideas: themselves, both, or the skill alone. It does not judge ideas until asked to converge. Sessions resume. | `{output_folder}/{active_initiative}/brainstorm-/`, or under `{output_folder}/` for loose work, with `brainstorm.html` and, on request, `brainstorm-.md`: the chosen ideas, ready as input to any installed planning skill. | | `bmad-forge-idea` | Questions one half-formed idea hard until the user can act on it or drop it. | Any idea, not only products, including a change to an existing project. It ends hardened, killed, or clearer, and all three are good outcomes. Not for generating ideas or for outside facts. | `{output_folder}/{active_initiative}/forge-/`, or under `{output_folder}/` for loose work, with `forge-report.html` and, when the idea hardens, `forge-.md`: the surviving decisions, ready as input to any installed planning or build skill. | | `bmad-deep-recon` | Research that serves a decision, with cited sources found now, never from memory. | It can draft a prompt for the user's own research tool, process a finished report, or run the research here. It can also choose between candidates, or answer questions about this repository from its code and git history. | `{output_folder}/{active_initiative}/research-/`, or under `{output_folder}/` for loose work, with `brief.md` and `research-.md`, which is input for whatever skill acts on the decision. Codebase research also writes each ADR the user approves, beside the code it governs. | | `bmad-facilitate` | Coaches the user through one document from a template library, then updates or validates it later. | Its templates come from installed modules: Method's `decision-record`, `postmortem` and `security-review`, Founder's `proposal` and `pitch-deck`, and the Creative Intelligence Suite's `character`, from CIS 0.4.0. A team adds or replaces templates and adds rules to shipped ones. Rigor follows the stakes the user states. Unfinished runs resume. With no fitting template it builds a structure and offers to save it. | `{output_folder}/{active_initiative}/-/`, or under `{output_folder}/` for loose work, with `-.md`, `.memlog.md`, review files and, when rendered, `-.html`. | | `bmad-advanced-elicitation` | Pushes a draft off its first answer and proposes a revision. | It names the draft and where it is weak and starts right away: a best-fit critique method and a wildcard (pre-mortem, steelman, first principles, red team, and more) as independent readers, plus an open push for a single choice or a second method for a document, then one proposed revision with each push's findings. Nothing changes unless the user accepts. It starts only when named, and a method named when invoking it runs straight away. | `{output_folder}/{active_initiative}/elicitation-/`, or under `{output_folder}/` for loose work, with each push's findings and a report of every round. The work itself changes only where the user accepts. | | `bmad-review` | Independent review lenses over any diff or document: adversarial, edge cases, verification gaps, structure, prose. | It runs only when the user asks and says "review". Acting on earlier findings is a change, not a review. No severity ranking. | The report in chat, or a file when the project sets a report path. | | `bmad-party-mode` | A group conversation between agents or personas, with the user in the room. | It works alone or beside any skill. Custom parties, a default party, and memory are all configurable, and a module can ship a cast. It debates and does not verify. | On request, a keepsake `{output_folder}/{active_initiative}/party-/party-.html`, or under `{output_folder}/` for loose work. Memory under `{output_folder}/party-mode/memories/`. | | `bmad-shard-pro` | Makes a long markdown or text document cheap for an agent to navigate: leaves it, adds a contents list, or splits it word for word into shards. | It may recommend not splitting, and never rewrites content. Any agent can change it later by following the note in its main file. | In the document's own folder: a main file named after the folder that links to every shard, the shards, and the frozen original in `.source/`. | | `bmad-ingest` | Turns raw input into a cited note an agent or person acts on instead of the raw: decisions, action items, open questions, key points. | The note's shape comes from a template; teams and modules add their own. Every item points back to the raw, and a review pass checks it. Other skills can call it on their inputs. | The original, unchanged, in `{output_folder}/raw/`; the note in the calling skill's folder, such as a PRD's `sources/`, else `{output_folder}/notes/`. | | `bmad-customize` | Changes how an installed skill or agent behaves without editing it: persona, standing facts, templates, output paths, steps on completion, and what a document such as the PRD asks for, contains or renders. | Team overrides are committed and shared; personal ones are not. It offers only what the target skill exposes. A document change extends its template, so updates to the original still arrive. Central config is edited by hand. | `{project-root}/_bmad/custom/{skill-name}.toml` for the team, `{skill-name}.user.toml` for one person; a document change in `{project-root}/_bmad/custom/facilitate-templates/`. | ## `bmad`: setup, status, and help - `bmad setup` creates and repairs `{project-root}/_bmad`, including the shared scripts other skills call, and asks each installed module's new configuration questions. Recommend it after anything is installed or updated. - `bmad status` changes nothing. It reports what is installed, what is missing or out of date, and the one command to run next. - Either takes a module code, such as `bmad setup core-tools`, to cover that module only. - To add a module that is not installed, such as the Test Architect, run `npx skills add bmad-code-org/bmad-method-test-architecture-enterprise`, then `bmad setup tea`. - BMad is installed per project. To use it in another repository, run `npx skills add bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD` there, then `bmad setup`. ## More detail This document should be enough to route the user and say what to do next. Each topic file below sits in this folder and goes deeper on one subject. Read one only when the question is about that subject, using the path the knowledge script lists for it. For how one skill behaves in detail, that skill's own files are the last resort. | Topic file | Read when the user asks about | |---|---| | `help/advanced-elicitation.md` | How to start and aim `bmad-advanced-elicitation`, what it runs when no methods are named, what comes back, default and custom methods, when a plain "push harder" is enough. | | `help/party-mode.md` | What party mode is good for alone or with other skills, custom parties, the default party, memory, parties that come with a module. | | `help/research.md` | Getting the most from `bmad-deep-recon` and which of its services to use. | | `help/facilitate.md` | What `bmad-facilitate` can write and how to list every template available here, so open it before saying what the user can be coached through. Also its shipped templates, calling it directly, a team's own templates and extensions. | | `help/customization.md` | How overrides work: team or personal file, how they merge, central config, an override that is not applied, resetting. | | `help/team-adoption.md` | Making a whole team's BMad follow shared rules, tools, templates, and publishing steps. | | `help/ingest.md` | Processing transcripts, threads, recordings or long reports, ingest's templates and adding them, where the original and the note go, ingest inside a PRD or other work, sensitive recordings. | | `help/shard-pro.md` | Whether to shard a document, contents list or split, how a sharded document works, `.source/`, changing one, handing one to another skill. | | `help/modules.md` | What a BMad module is, each file in one, a single-skill module, a module that only ships personas and parties, building one. | ## When this document is not enough For a `core-tools` question this document, its topic files, and the installed skills cannot answer, fetch the documentation site at `https://docs.bmad-method.org/` and follow the pages relevant to the question. The source repository it links to is the final authority on how anything actually behaves. === DOC {'module': 'method', 'path': 'help/help.md', 'skills': ['bmad-agent-analyst', 'bmad-agent-architect', 'bmad-agent-dev', 'bmad-agent-pm', 'bmad-agent-po', 'bmad-agent-ux-designer', 'bmad-architecture', 'bmad-build', 'bmad-build-auto', 'bmad-code-review', 'bmad-project-context', 'bmad-qa-generate-e2e-tests', 'bmad-retrospective', 'bmad-ux', 'bmad-walkthrough'], 'installed_skills': ['bmad-agent-analyst', 'bmad-agent-architect', 'bmad-agent-dev', 'bmad-agent-pm', 'bmad-agent-po', 'bmad-agent-ux-designer', 'bmad-architecture', 'bmad-build', 'bmad-build-auto', 'bmad-code-review', 'bmad-project-context', 'bmad-qa-generate-e2e-tests', 'bmad-retrospective', 'bmad-ux', 'bmad-walkthrough'], 'reported_from': 'bmod-method'} # BMad Method knowledge This document covers the skills of the `method` module: what each one gives the user, when to recommend it, and what to offer next. ## How the method works The method turns an intent of any size into working software. Recommend the smallest path that safely fits the work; never march the user through every skill. A project may hold only some of these skills: recommend from what is installed, and say plainly when a step has no installed skill rather than inventing a substitute. **The ticket is the spec.** The initiative, epic or story file is the spec at its level. Every skill that works on a ticket reads it first and in full and trusts it; its `sources:` are re-read only by Sofia when she updates it, and a `companions:` file only where the ticket points. Talk to Sofia the Product Owner (`bmad-agent-po`) to fill its Requirements from whatever the user has (a PRD, a brief, notes, a transcript), keep it in step with its sources, and slice from it. A transcript, a chat or email thread, or a voice memo goes through `bmad-ingest` first when it is installed, and the note it returns is the input. A sharded document is given to any skill as its main file, named after its folder, which links to every shard. The method adds note templates for `standup`, `retrospective` (the meeting, not `bmad-retrospective`'s epic review), `sprint-review`, `discovery-workshop` and `user-interview`. The four phases are analysis (ideation, research, is it worth building), planning (what exactly, and in what slices), implementation (build it), and validation (is it right). They describe what kind of help a skill gives. They are not a mandatory sequence to complete. Project size decides how many build sessions the work needs. Stakes decide how heavy the planning gets. A large hobby project keeps planning light; a small change to a regulated system may not. ## More detail This document should be enough to route the user and say what to do next. Each topic file below sits in this folder and goes deeper on one subject. Read one only when the question is about that subject, using the path the knowledge script lists for it. | Topic file | Read when the user asks about | |---|---| | `help/analysis-skills.md` | The brief or the PRFAQ from Mary (`bmad-agent-analyst`) in depth: what each gives, when to pick it, when not to, how they relate. | | `help/planning-skills.md` | `bmad-agent-po` (Sofia), `bmad-agent-pm` (John) and his planning documents, `bmad-ux`, `bmad-architecture` in depth, and customizing John's templates. | | `help/implementation-skills.md` | `bmad-build` or `bmad-build-auto` in depth. | | `help/validation-skills.md` | `bmad-code-review`, `bmad-walkthrough`, `bmad-qa-generate-e2e-tests`, or `bmad-retrospective` in depth. | | `help/prototyping.md` | Prototyping or vibe coding first, what a prototype is good for (worth doing, feasibility, complexity, unknowns), non-engineers prototyping, what to do with a prototype afterwards, whether planning still matters after a good first version. | | `help/existing-codebase.md` | Using BMad on an inherited, brownfield, or long-lived codebase. | | `help/preparing-a-repo-for-agents.md` | Getting a codebase ready for agentic coding, inconsistent agent output, how much documentation to keep (small ADRs, not heavy docs), regular refactoring, holding quality over time. | | `help/artifact-lifetime.md` | Whether to keep PRDs, specs, stories, and build records after the work is done, archiving, closing out an epic, keeping old plans from misleading agents. | | `help/monorepo-and-polyrepo.md` | Where to install BMad and keep planning when work spans one repository or several; the workspace layout for a poly repo. | | `help/working-in-an-organization.md` | A team or enterprise: an existing PRD, Jira or another tracker, approvals and sign-off, document owners, several engineers in parallel, requirements changing mid-flight. | | `help/ticketing-and-epics.md` | How Sofia's ticket tree works (initiatives, planning an epic's stories, the breakdown, building from an entry, refining), plan status, review, and retrospective. | | `help/ticketing-setup.md` | Setting up and driving the ticket tree with Sofia: the store, several repos, trackers, the phrases to say, the hand-off to `bmad-build`. | | `help/unattended-builds.md` | `bmad-build-auto`, building stories with no human present, a blocked run and how to retry, what to check after a run. | | `help/review-choices.md` | Review depth, skipping review, another review pass, when to stop, slow reviews, customizing review. | | `help/project-context.md` | `bmad-project-context` in depth: what belongs in `AGENTS.md`, why the block is small, its intents, removing a rule. | ## Routing Every "what next" is answered by the state of the spec at its altitude: the initiative file, then each epic file. # Company Room Booking

## Description

One web app where anyone in the company finds a free meeting room in London, Manchester or Leeds and books it, with double bookings made impossible. It replaces the three per-office spreadsheets and rooms named in calendar invites, which grew unworkable this year as the company reached three offices and more people came back in. Release one has no accounts and no outside calendars: people pick their name, book, and see their bookings in a built-in calendar; office managers keep their office's rooms current. Inputs: the final brief, PRD and UX (References).

## Outcome

About 300 staff and their office managers find and book rooms in one trusted place instead of three spreadsheets, shown by PRD SM-1 to SM-3 and watched by the SM-4 stop signal and the SM-5 counter-metric.

## Requirements

- R1 (FR-1): A person picks their name from the loaded people and then uses the app as that person, with their name shown throughout.
- R2 (FR-2): A person can switch to another name at any time; the picked name is remembered on that device until they switch.
- R3 (FR-3): An office manager adds a room to their office, with at least a name and a capacity.
- R4 (FR-4): An office manager edits a room in their office.
- R5 (FR-5, RULE-5): An office manager closes and reopens a room in their office; a closed room shows as closed and cannot be booked.
- R6 (FR-6): A person chooses an office, a date, a start time and a length and sees which of that office's rooms are free, on a laptop and on a phone, for any time, not only from now; their home office is shown first and any office can be chosen.
- R7 (FR-7, UJ-1): A person books a free room by giving a start time, a length from 15 minutes to 4 hours, a title and attendees from the loaded people; they become its organiser, and the booking shows in their calendar and every attendee's.
- R8 (FR-8): Any booking, or change to a booking, that would overlap another booking of the same room is refused, and the person is told why.
- R9 (FR-9): The organiser changes a booking's room, start time, length, title or attendees under the same rules as a new booking.
- R10 (FR-10): An office manager changes any booking of a room in their office under the same rules as R9.
- R11 (FR-11): The organiser, or an office manager of the room's office, cancels a booking, and the room shows as free to everyone at once.
- R12 (FR-12): A person sees their own bookings, both those they organise and those they attend, in a built-in calendar by day and by week.
- R13 (FR-13): From their calendar a person opens one of their bookings and changes or cancels it when RULE-3 allows.
- R14 (FR-14): A person moves their calendar to the previous or next day or week.
- R15 (EXPERIENCE Booking Visibility): Everyone sees a booking's room, time, title and organiser; its attendees are shown only to the organiser, the attendees and office managers of the room's office.
- R16 (EXPERIENCE Interaction Primitives): A person books a free room in three taps or fewer, with no typing required.

## Constraints

- RULE-1, PRD Decisions: Two bookings of the same room never overlap in time; there is no override, for office managers either.
- RULE-2: A booking lasts from 15 minutes to 4 hours; start times and lengths move in 15-minute steps.
- RULE-3: Only a booking's organiser and the office managers of the room's office may change or cancel it.
- RULE-4: Only office managers may add, edit, close or reopen rooms, and only in their own office, which is their home office.
- RULE-6: No accounts or passwords in release one; anyone can pick anyone's name, and every booking shows its organiser.
- RULE-7: Built with Python, FastAPI and SQLite; the user's computer is for building and testing, and where it runs for the company is decided in the architecture.
- RULE-8: Free rooms for a given office and time are visible in under 10 seconds from opening the app.
- RULE-9: Every feature works in a browser on a laptop and on a phone.
- PRD Quality and constraints: One time zone, UK time, for all three offices.
- PRD Decisions, Rollout: Before go-live office managers check their office's rooms are in the app and correct; at go-live the spreadsheets are frozen and organisers re-enter their own future bookings, so no spreadsheet import is built.
- User, 2026-11-12: Offices, people, home offices and office-manager marks load from a seed file while building; HR supplies the real list before go-live, and it loads the same way.

## Done when

- All five capabilities (picking your name, rooms, finding a free room, booking, my calendar) are live for London, Manchester and Leeds, reachable on laptop and phone where the company hosts the app.
- Zero overlapping bookings after go-live (SM-1).
- A person sees a free room for a given office and time in under 10 seconds from opening the app (SM-2).
- No office uses its spreadsheet for new bookings four weeks after go-live (SM-3).
- Office managers report no bookings made or changed under someone's name without them in the first six weeks, or sign-in is brought forward (SM-5).

## Boundaries

Release one only. Out, per PRD Non-goals and MVP scope:

- Check-in at the room and freeing no-show rooms (the next release).
- Visitors or bookings for people outside the company.
- Catering, equipment requests and room set-up.
- Desk booking, displays outside rooms and usage reports.
- Links to outside calendars: no Outlook, Google or other sync, invites or feeds.
- Notifications of any kind.
- Accounts, passwords or sign-in, including single sign-on.
- Loading or editing people or offices inside the app.
- Recurring bookings.
- Touch point: none. The app is standalone and connects to no calendar, directory or other system.
- Tracer path: a person picks their name, sees free rooms in their office, books one with attendees, finds it in their and the attendees' calendars, then changes or cancels it, while an office manager closes a room and it stops showing as free.

- Assumption: A person's calendar includes bookings they attend, not only those they organise (R12, PRD A4).

- Open question: Go-live date (PRD OQ-1). Owner: user. Blocks rollout planning.
- Open question: How long past bookings are kept, and what data-protection duty applies to staff names and attendee lists (PRD OQ-3); also decides whether a cancelled booking stays deleted (architecture AD-13). Owner: user. Needed before go-live.
- Open question: Which host runs the app, and can it be reached only from company networks (office Wi-Fi, VPN) as architecture AD-11 assumes, since there is no sign-in (PRD OQ-4, narrowed by AD-11). Owner: user with IT. Blocks epic-offices-and-rooms' deployment story, not its other stories.
- Open question: What happens to a closed room's future bookings (PRD FR-5). Owner: epic-find-and-book.
- Decision: 2026-11-12, user: the first epic is offices and rooms, because nothing can be booked until rooms exist; the platform baseline is its first stories. Sofia's default would have opened on the booking path, the riskiest (RULE-1 under concurrent bookings); the user's order also lets office managers enter and check rooms on the live app before go-live, as the rollout asks.
- Decision: 2026-11-12, user: approved three epics in build order: offices and rooms, find and book, my calendar (tickets/tickets.toml).
- Decision: 2026-11-12, user: the fate of a closed room's future bookings moves from the rooms epic to epic-find-and-book, because bookings exist only there; epic 1's close only marks the room closed.
- Decision: 2026-11-12: shared decisions (hosting, rendering, data model, UK time, overlap enforcement under concurrent bookings, the remembered name, the office-manager check) go to a bmad-architecture spine before epic 1 is built.

# Company Room Booking

## Description

One web app where anyone in the company finds a free meeting room in London, Manchester or Leeds and books it, with double bookings made impossible. It replaces the three per-office spreadsheets and rooms named in calendar invites, which grew unworkable this year as the company reached three offices and more people came back in. Release one has no accounts and no outside calendars: people pick their name, book, and see their bookings in a built-in calendar; office managers keep their office's rooms current. Inputs: the final brief, PRD and UX (References).

## Outcome

About 300 staff and their office managers find and book rooms in one trusted place instead of three spreadsheets, shown by PRD SM-1 to SM-3 and watched by the SM-4 stop signal and the SM-5 counter-metric.

## Requirements

- R1 (FR-1): A person picks their name from the loaded people and then uses the app as that person, with their name shown throughout.
- R2 (FR-2): A person can switch to another name at any time; the picked name is remembered on that device until they switch.
- R3 (FR-3): An office manager adds a room to their office, with at least a name and a capacity.
- R4 (FR-4): An office manager edits a room in their office.
- R5 (FR-5, RULE-5): An office manager closes and reopens a room in their office; a closed room shows as closed and cannot be booked.
- R6 (FR-6): A person chooses an office, a date, a start time and a length and sees which of that office's rooms are free, on a laptop and on a phone, for any time, not only from now; their home office is shown first and any office can be chosen.
- R7 (FR-7, UJ-1): A person books a free room by giving a start time, a length from 15 minutes to 4 hours, a title and attendees from the loaded people; they become its organiser, and the booking shows in their calendar and every attendee's.
- R8 (FR-8): Any booking, or change to a booking, that would overlap another booking of the same room is refused, and the person is told why.
- R9 (FR-9): The organiser changes a booking's room, start time, length, title or attendees under the same rules as a new booking.
- R10 (FR-10): An office manager changes any booking of a room in their office under the same rules as R9.
- R11 (FR-11): The organiser, or an office manager of the room's office, cancels a booking, and the room shows as free to everyone at once.
- R12 (FR-12): A person sees their own bookings, both those they organise and those they attend, in a built-in calendar by day and by week.
- R13 (FR-13): From their calendar a person opens one of their bookings and changes or cancels it when RULE-3 allows.
- R14 (FR-14): A person moves their calendar to the previous or next day or week.
- R15 (EXPERIENCE Booking Visibility): Everyone sees a booking's room, time, title and organiser; its attendees are shown only to the organiser, the attendees and office managers of the room's office.
- R16 (EXPERIENCE Interaction Primitives): A person books a free room in three taps or fewer, with no typing required.

## Constraints

- RULE-1, PRD Decisions: Two bookings of the same room never overlap in time; there is no override, for office managers either.
- RULE-2: A booking lasts from 15 minutes to 4 hours; start times and lengths move in 15-minute steps.
- RULE-3: Only a booking's organiser and the office managers of the room's office may change or cancel it.
- RULE-4: Only office managers may add, edit, close or reopen rooms, and only in their own office, which is their home office.
- RULE-6: No accounts or passwords in release one; anyone can pick anyone's name, and every booking shows its organiser.
- RULE-7: Built with Python, FastAPI and SQLite; the user's computer is for building and testing, and where it runs for the company is decided in the architecture.
- RULE-8: Free rooms for a given office and time are visible in under 10 seconds from opening the app.
- RULE-9: Every feature works in a browser on a laptop and on a phone.
- PRD Quality and constraints: One time zone, UK time, for all three offices.
- PRD Decisions, Rollout: Before go-live office managers check their office's rooms are in the app and correct; at go-live the spreadsheets are frozen and organisers re-enter their own future bookings, so no spreadsheet import is built.
- User, 2026-11-12: Offices, people, home offices and office-manager marks load from a seed file while building; HR supplies the real list before go-live, and it loads the same way.

## Done when

- All five capabilities (picking your name, rooms, finding a free room, booking, my calendar) are live for London, Manchester and Leeds, reachable on laptop and phone where the company hosts the app.
- Zero overlapping bookings after go-live (SM-1).
- A person sees a free room for a given office and time in under 10 seconds from opening the app (SM-2).
- No office uses its spreadsheet for new bookings four weeks after go-live (SM-3).
- Office managers report no bookings made or changed under someone's name without them in the first six weeks, or sign-in is brought forward (SM-5).

## Boundaries

Release one only. Out, per PRD Non-goals and MVP scope:

- Check-in at the room and freeing no-show rooms (the next release).
- Visitors or bookings for people outside the company.
- Catering, equipment requests and room set-up.
- Desk booking, displays outside rooms and usage reports.
- Links to outside calendars: no Outlook, Google or other sync, invites or feeds.
- Notifications of any kind.
- Accounts, passwords or sign-in, including single sign-on.
- Loading or editing people or offices inside the app.
- Recurring bookings.
- Touch point: none. The app is standalone and connects to no calendar, directory or other system.
- Tracer path: a person picks their name, sees free rooms in their office, books one with attendees, finds it in their and the attendees' calendars, then changes or cancels it, while an office manager closes a room and it stops showing as free.

## Description

The heart of the initiative: on laptop and phone, a person sees which rooms in any office are free for any date, time and length, books one with attendees in three taps or fewer, and the organiser or an office manager changes or cancels it. # Board

Read a ticket, and its remote state if published, before changing it. Commit changed files on the current branch when `output_folder` is in a git repo; never push.

`tickets.py --help` on a command gives its arguments and output keys.



## Reading the tree

- `find`'s `<ref>` is `<epic id>.<entry id>`, an entry id with its epic folder, a tracker id, a file name, or an unbroken title phrase; for looser words, pick from `status`, asking when several fit. Its `story_file` is null until pulled; `plan` is the plan's path, existing or not.
- `tickets.py next [<folder>]` groups open tickets by next step; `tickets.py status [<folder>]` lists every ticket.
- `<folder>` is an epic folder name, `backlog`, or the initiative, by default the active one, where `next` and `status` add a `backlog` key to show. On a parent initiative they list its child initiatives under `initiatives`.
- With a tracker, sync first (Tracker sync) and pass `--synced` to `next`.

Act with the user on any non-empty key:

- `unpinned_after`: add the epic's `after` prerequisite to the entry that needs it.
- `undeclared_after`: add the awaited epic, with its `needs`, to its epic's `after` in the breakdown, or drop the prerequisite.
- `order_conflict`: reorder or merge the epics, or record why in a `Decision:` line.
- `drift`: make the leaf file's and the entry's `after` or `hitl` equal.
- `problems`: an orphan plan gets its `ticket` set to the entry id or file stem; an unknown status is fixed with `mark`.
- `waiting_on` on a `blocked` row: say what the ticket waits on.
- `unknown` on a `blocked` row: settle it, remove it, and add a dated `Decision:` line to the file's Notes, or its epic's when it has no file.

## Publish

On the repo store, approval commits (Conventions in `workflow.md`) and `publication` does not apply. On a tracker, publication is `at_inception`: `at_inception` offers to publish the agreed set after validation; `on_start` publishes each ticket when it starts. An explicit user request overrides it.

Publish to a tracker through `write`:

- Write the leaf's file first (`tickets.py pull` if none); send it minus the frontmatter lines `tracker_id`, `remote`, `tracker_status`, `status`, and `assignee`.
- Create parents and prerequisites first, adding local prerequisites to the scope. An `after` naming a sibling's id or `<epic id>.<entry id>` is that entry's remote item; `epic-<slug>` is the epic's.
- A type mapped to `""` is never sent; its children attach to the nearest published ancestor. Say so once.
- Offer `setup` at first publish, or when the tracker lacks something the maps or `fields` name.
- Then mirror, and edit a published container's `tracker_id` and `remote` into its file.

An unrefined ticket may be published with `refined: false`; refinement updates the same file and remote item.

## Start

Offer the first `ready_to_start` row of `next` in build order, or every unassigned one when work can run in parallel. `find` it with the row's `ref`, refine a `ready_to_refine` one first per `ticket.md`, and confirm it is unassigned; the builder reads the ticket. With the user's approval, start it: on a tracker, publish it if needed, `write` it to `[tickets.status].in-progress` and mirror; on the repo store, write nothing. Then hand it to `bmad-build` or `bmad-build-auto`.

Only an unattended run's orchestrator honors the row's `plan_checkpoint` and `done_checkpoint`.

## Status

The plan is `<type>-<slug>-plan.md` beside where the leaf's file is or would be, linked by its `ticket`; the leaf file's `status` counts only without a plan.

The builds write `draft` through `built`, and `bmad-build-auto` writes `blocked` when it halts; an orchestrator may set `done` through `mark`. Sofia sets `done`, `dropped`, or an assignee only when the user says so (a ticket done or dropped, or a person working it by hand).

- **Repo store.** `tickets.py mark [<folder>] <ref> <status> [--assignee <who>] [--blocked <reason>]`, then commit. `mark` writes only the plan; the checks here are yours.
